title: Thinning out Steiner trees: a node-based model for uniform edge costs
contribution: A node-only MIP model for Steiner tree problems with uniform edge costs, solved by a deliberately simple branch-and-cut (lazy minimal-separator cuts on integer points only, no fractional separation) inside a local-branching and Benders-like set-covering heuristic framework, which proved optimality in seconds on previously unsolved uniform SteinLib instances (GAPS s1-s5, SP w13c29 and w23c23) and improved the best known values of hard PUC and I640 instances for the 2014 DIMACS challenge (read on the preprint, the DIMACS 11 version).
problem_entry: Public instances still unsolved by state-of-the-art branch-and-cut codes; instead of enriching the polyhedral description, take 'the opposite viewpoint' and test the hypothesis that their hardness comes from over-modelling, on the class where edge models carry many equivalent trees (uniform edge costs) (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Drop the edge variables: binary node variables with the uniform edge cost shifted into node costs, connectivity by node-separator inequalities enforced lazily on integer points, plus node-degree and 2-cycle inequalities; keep the B&C simple and put the effort into primal machinery (asymmetric local branching with restarts and a global cut pool, recombination, a Benders-like set-covering heuristic whose 'blurred' relaxation feeds a repair B&C) (pp. 4-11).
assumptions: Generalised PCSTP on an undirected graph with possibly empty real terminals, edge costs and node revenues; potential terminals from a leaf argument; the y-model needs uniform edge costs (general costs by an untested edge-splitting remark); STP, (rooted) PCSTP, MWCS via its PCSTP form, DC-STP; hard SteinLib (PUC, I640, GAPS, SP, LIN, ...) and DIMACS MWCS instances; set-covering structure of pure STP and bipartite graphs with many terminals exploited; correctness by cutting off every infeasible integer point in a LazyCutCallback (pp. 2-7, 11-12, 15, 17, 19).
proof_devices: Lemma 1 (a node separator is minimal iff each of its nodes touches both components; from Golumbic [14]) and Proposition 1: Algorithm 1 (delete the edges inside C_i and A(C_i), BFS from j that never queues A(C_i), return A(C_i) ∩ R_j) returns a minimal (i, j) separator in O(|E|), pp. 5-6

Validity without fractional separation: every infeasible integer point, including those from CPLEX's heuristics, cut off by a LazyCutCallback; max-flow fractional separation described and switched off as too slow, p. 5
Node-degree inequalities (5), valid and not implied by (2), strengthened to minimal separators and lifted for potential terminals; 2-cycle inequalities (6), pp. 4-5
Leaf argument: some optimal PCSTP solution has no zero-revenue leaf and no leaf whose cheapest edge costs more than its revenue, which defines potential terminals, pp. 2-3
Orbit argument on hypercubes: one orbit holds all non-terminal variables, so one Steiner node may be fixed to 1 without loss of generality; deliberately not applied, p. 15

Global pool of lazily separated cuts re-added before every B&C restart so that presolve and {0,1/2}-cuts act; restarts with changed seeds; recombination B&C on the union of the best solutions every ten iterations, Algorithm 2, pp. 7-8
Asymmetric local branching constraint (7), radius 10-20, solution limit and deterministic time limit per call, radius schedule r_min, r_delta, r_max, Algorithm 3, pp. 8-9

Benders-like set-covering heuristic (Algorithm 4): extracted set-covering relaxation solved by CFT, repair by radius-0 asymmetric local branching (fixing) and a short B&C, violated cuts fed back; row and column shuffling and 20% random skipping of fixings; blurred node weights for non-uniform bipartite instances, pp. 9-12
Filter rules on |E|/|V| < 3, |T|/|V| > 0.4, uniformity, bipartiteness and weight range < 10 choosing model, tailing-off and initialization heuristic, Tables 1-2, pp. 13-14

(x, y)-model: aggregated asymmetry constraints stronger than those of [19]; max-flow cuts one terminal at a time with capacity updates, cut-sets near the terminal; branching on tailing-off; GSECs for infeasible integer points, p. 15
experiments: All nontrivial DIMACS instances first run by the plain exact B&C, 1 h, fixed seed; unsolved ones are 'difficult' and get the heuristic framework, 1 h, 10 seeds (BEST/AVG/STD); cluster of 20-core 2.3 GHz nodes with up to five 4-core runs per node (stated slowdown), CPLEX 12.6 (memory limit 16 GB in the text, 12 GB in the appendix), wall-clock. Table 3 preliminary TURNI-binary results (5 of 7 improved); Table 4: y-model proves GAPS s1-s5 optimal in 0.03-30.06 s where the (x, y)-model keeps 1.19-3.02% gaps after 7,200 s, SP w13c29 and w23c23 solved for the first time, a single run with seed 0 although 'very erratic'; Table 5 MWCS best of five, y-model loses on the mice instances (3,758.1 s vs 1.2 s); Table 6 improvements only (e.g. hc12p -682); appendix prints all instances incl. y-model memouts (7 of 13 PUCN, 7 of 18 PUCNU) and heuristic values worse than the previous best (10 of 15 I640 STP, 11 of 13 LIN, cc12-2p +2947), my counts (pp. 12, 16-18, 22, 42, 49-50).
positioning: Against polyhedral enrichment; credits the node-based MWCS lineage (Backes et al. [3], improved by node separators in [1]); the toolbox is largely the authors' own (10 of 21 references carry Fischetti's name: local branching, proximity search, restarts, {0,1/2}-cuts, CFT, TURNI, the 2006 PCSTP framework; two more by the Vienna co-authors); local branching presented as LNS-like and of 'a primal nature'; states what it changed in the fallback (x, y)-model; yardstick the DIMACS best-bounds file (pp. 1, 3, 7-9, 15, 18, 20-21, 49).
writing: Contrarian abstract ('the opposite viewpoint') with a named working hypothesis, the 'thinning out' and 'agile framework' metaphors and a hedge ('Even though we do not claim our approach can work well in all cases'); surprise flagged ('To our pleasant surprise'); preliminary results printed as such before the final ones; a 'blurred' relaxation; one-paragraph conclusion; detail in a 30-page appendix (pp. 1, 11, 16, 18-19, 22-51).
limits_future: No claim for all cases; fractional separation too slow; LP relaxation too slow on very large uniform instances; sequential CFT; one-hour values improve with time and threads; tables show y-model memouts, losses on mice and heuristic values worse than the previous best on LIN and I640; future: edge splitting for general costs, possibly on the fly (pp. 1, 5, 10-11, 17-19, 22, 42, 49-50).

method_links.note: The thin model is the thesis: edge variables dropped under uniform costs, connectivity enforced lazily; a filter on cheap features picks the model that fits the instance class (y-model for uniform, (x, y)-model otherwise) and thin and fat models are measured on the same instances; the thin model loses on mice and runs out of memory on PUCN, so the choice is per class; for the heuristic the model is thinned further into a blurred set-covering relaxation

Stock CPLEX 12.6 does most of the work: one LazyCutCallback, no fractional separation, the cut pool re-added so that CPLEX's presolve and {0,1/2}-cuts act; local branching uses the MIP solver as a black box; the first set-covering test ran the existing TURNI binary off-line through text files before CFT was written into the code

Variability exploited (restarts with new seeds, shuffling, random skipping of fixings, seeds on parallel cores) and reported (BEST/AVG/STD over 10 seeds, best of five on MWCS), but no placebo arm, and Table 4 is one run with seed 0 although its larger instances are called very erratic

Difficulty defined in advance by a fixed-seed run of the plain exact code; thin and fat models in the same framework with the fat (x, y)-model given two hours; the appendix prints every nontrivial instance, losses included. Lapses: Table 6 lists only improvements, the yardstick is a best-bounds file from other codes and machines, shared nodes slow the runs

The cut loop is shortened (no fractional separation in the y-model, branching on tailing-off in the (x, y)-model) and the separated cut-set is changed (one terminal at a time with capacity updates, cut-sets near the terminal); the separated point is not moved

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: inexact model to search, true model to accept
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The set-covering 'relaxation' keeps only y(S) >= 1 rows, is solved heuristically by CFT and, for non-uniform costs, on blurred node weights; it is not meant to give bounds, only to propose fixings that a B&C on the true model with the original costs repairs, and the cuts found make the proposal infeasible next time. Same shape in S059 (this batch); cf. the S023 card ('blurring', batch c07) and the S164 card ('decouple the search LP from the certificate LP', batch c13)

The framework is assembled from the authors' earlier components (local branching, proximity-search radius advice, multiple restarts, {0,1/2}-cuts, the CFT heuristic, the TURNI binary); 10 of 21 references carry Fischetti's name and two more are by the Vienna co-authors

transferable: Shift a uniform edge cost into node costs (c_v = c - p_v) and model connectivity with node variables only (p. 4).
Separate only infeasible integer points, in linear time: a BFS from j that never queues the neighbours of i's component returns a minimal violated separator (Algorithm 1, Proposition 1, pp. 5-6).
Re-add a global pool of lazily separated cuts before each B&C restart so that presolve and the solver's general cuts work on an explicit formulation (p. 7).
Run asymmetric local branching with a small radius (10-20), a solution limit and a deterministic time limit per call; enlarge the radius after a failure, reset it after a success (pp. 8-9).
Every ten local-branching iterations, solve a B&C on the subgraph induced by the union of the best solutions (p. 7).
Benders-like repair: solve a relaxation heuristically, fix what it selects, repair with a short B&C, feed the violated cuts back, repeat (Algorithm 4, pp. 9-11).
Make a deterministic heuristic seed-dependent by shuffling rows and columns and skipping 20% of the fixings at random, and run seeds in parallel, one per core (p. 11).
Encode 'the model that fits the instance' as an explicit filter on cheap instance features (sparsity, terminal ratio, uniformity, bipartiteness, weight range) (Tables 1-2, pp. 13-14).
Define 'difficult' by a fixed-seed run of the plain exact code before the heuristic campaign, then report best, mean and standard deviation over 10 seeds (pp. 12, 18, 49).
On (almost) uniform instances with many symmetric solutions, let local search accept non-decreasing moves (p. 14).
Prototype with an existing binary off-line, through text files, before embedding the component, and print those preliminary numbers next to the final ones (pp. 16, 18).
Give the rival model the longer time limit when the claim is that your model is faster (two hours, Table 4, p. 17).
coauthors: M. Leitner, I. Ljubić, M. Luipersbeck, M. Monaci, M. Resch, D. Salvagnin, M. Sinnl (alphabetical list with Fischetti; Padova and Vienna)

quotes.text: Our working hypothesis is instead that the extreme hardness of some classes of instances mainly comes from over-modeling, and that some instances can become quite easy to solve when a simpler model is considered.

one can think of the relaxation as a “blurred” version of the original problem, which retains some of its main features but is not bothered by too many details (namely, connectivity conditions) that would overload the model.

title: Using a general-purpose mixed-integer linear programming solver for the practical solution of real-time train rescheduling
contribution: A feasibility study for Alstom showing that stock CPLEX 12.6.2 on the standard alternative-graph rescheduling MILP misses the 2-10 s real-time limits, but meets them on 28 real instances (feasible on 26 with 8 standard PCs, on all 28 with a 50% faster PC emulated by longer limits, against 12 of 28 without the additions) once a possibly invalid bound on the maximum delay and route fixing are added as heuristic preprocessing and runs are diversified over independent PCs (read on the author preprint of February 5, 2017).
problem_entry: An industrial yes/no question (can a modern general-purpose MILP solver do real-time rescheduling in practice?), answered by first re-measuring the plain solver against Alstom's 2/5/10 s limits, which it misses (13 of 29 within the target even with 10 PCs) (pp. 2, 4-5).
key_idea: Two heuristic preprocessing steps on top of an unchanged model and solver: a possibly invalid upper bound on the maximum-delay variable z_omega, which the solver's own presolve propagates into fixed binaries and smaller big-Ms, walked upward over a fixed ladder with presolve as the fast infeasibility test; and route fixing (ideal or random routes); found by testing many ideas and then removing features until two remained (pp. 5-8).
assumptions: Event-based job-shop MILP on an alternative graph with big-M disjunctions (route binaries, precedence binaries, times, delays, z_omega the maximum delay), objective average delay; 29 Alstom instances of simulated disruptions on a line near London (15/30/60-min horizons, 32-90 trains, 40-128 routes), MILP files from D'Ariano et al. (2014), instance 28 dropped; the objective drives z_omega towards its minimum on these instances; bound and route fixing are restrictions, so no optimality claim (pp. 2-7, 12-13).
proof_devices: Possibly invalid bound z_omega <= UB_omega on the maximum-delay variable, exploited by CPLEX's own presolve and propagation to fix binaries and reduce big-M coefficients; infeasible values detected almost immediately, p. 6

UB ladder 600, 900, 1200, 2000, 2500, 3000, 4000, 5000, +infinity: each CPLEX call gets the remaining wall-clock time and the next value is tried only when CPLEX proves infeasibility; at most 7 values, below 0.2 s of preprocessing, counted in the times, p. 8
Own longest-path infeasibility check removed because CPLEX's preprocessing detected infeasible bounds as fast, pp. 6-7

One run index s drives three diversifiers: CPLEX random seed, aggressive presolve (CPX_PARAM_PRESLVND = 3) for odd s, and route fixing (none for s in {1, 8}, ideal routes for s = 2, random routes for s = 3..7), p. 8
Independent runs on N_PC machines without communication, best value at the time limit kept; opportunistic parallel mode chosen because speed matters more than reproducibility, pp. 7-8
experiments: Baseline CPLEX 12.6.2 default and a heuristic setting (cuts off), 10 seeds each, best of 10 as a simulated 10-PC run, 1 h, Xeon E3-1220V2 3.1 GHz: feasible within the target on 13 of 29 at best. Method on a 2011 i7-2820QM 2.3 GHz, N_PC in {1, 4, 8}, 1 or 4 threads, metric best value / best known at the 2/5/10 s limit, '50% Faster PC' columns at 3/7/15 s; ablation arm with the same parameters and layout, features off. Results: 16 cases with one PC, 26 with 8 standard PCs, all 28 with the faster PC vs 12 of 28 without the features; one case worse with more PCs; D'Ariano et al. (2014) not comparable. My checks: Table 2's 8/4 column also has ratios 3.62 and 84.16 beyond the 'only 3 cases about 2' sentence; Table 1 rows 14 and 29 identical; no separate tuning set (pp. 4-11).
positioning: Explicit non-claim: no comparison with, and no claim to beat, ad-hoc methods (many proprietary); similar methods acknowledged; model credited to Mascis and Pacciarelli, D'Ariano et al. and Mannino and Mascis on Balas's disjunctive formulation; big-M reduction to Belotti et al. (co-authored); erraticism to Fischetti and Monaci and Lodi and Tramontani; verdict on the rival: both methods viable (pp. 2-6, 11).
writing: Partner's question answered 'essentially in the affirmative'; surprise flagged ('to our own pleasant surprise'); the paper presented as a lesson ('train rescheduling can become much easier once an apparently trivial preprocessing step is applied'); short text with the model in an appendix; small slips (#rows/#cols inverted, constraint numbers) (pp. 2-4, 13).
limits_future: No comparison with ad-hoc methods; meeting all limits rests on an assumed 50% faster processor; train categories ignored and objective restricted to average delay; future: other rescheduling contexts, train priorities, non-convex step functions of punctuality (pp. 3, 9, 11).

method_links.note: Stock CPLEX on the plain standard model first, in default and heuristic settings with 10 seeds each, misses the limits; the additions are one bound and route fixings on top of the unchanged solver in default mode; the authors' own infeasibility check was dropped because CPLEX's presolve was as fast; work stopped once the limits were met. The sub-decision is handed to presolve as a bound, not written as an auxiliary MIP

Ablation by subtraction: after a satisfactory implementation, features were disabled or simplified until two simple preprocessing operations remained; route fixing thins the model. The paper does not give the number of ideas tried nor say that removing the others improved performance (SKILL.md takes both from the TRI16 deck)

Erraticism used as a resource (best of 10 seeds per CPLEX setting; one run index drives seed, route fixing and presolve over non-communicating PCs), but no spread or placebo arm is reported, reproducibility is traded for speed by the opportunistic parallel mode, and more PCs once gave a worse solution

Ablation arm with the same CPLEX parameters, hardware and 8-PC layout, only the two features off; baseline includes the heuristic CPLEX setting a practitioner would try; the non-comparison with ad-hoc and rival methods is stated. Lapses: no separate tuning set for the ladder or the seed scheme, Table 1 on a different machine, the text-table mismatch and the twin rows of Table 1

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: a single heuristic bound that the solver's presolve propagates
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A tight, possibly invalid bound on the maximum-delay variable makes CPLEX's own preprocessing tighten many domains, fix many binaries and reduce big-Ms; infeasible bounds are detected almost at once, so an upward ladder of bounds costs under 0.2 s

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: inexact model to search, true model to accept
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The solver searches a restricted model (bound on z_omega, fixed routes); by construction its solutions are feasible for the original model, and the restriction is loosened only when presolve proves it infeasible. Same shape as S040's blurred set-covering relaxation in this batch

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: one seed, several diversifiers, no communication
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The run index s sets the CPLEX seed, the route-fixing rule (none, ideal, random) and aggressive presolve for odd s; runs on separate PCs never communicate and the best value at the time limit is taken

transferable: Measure the stock solver first, in default and in a heuristic setting, k seeds each, and read best-of-k as what k parallel machines would get (pp. 4-5).
Look for the one variable bound that drives presolve; impose it heuristically and walk a fixed ladder of values upward, each call getting the remaining time (pp. 6, 8).
Drop your own checks when the solver's presolve detects the same thing as fast (pp. 6-7).
Diversify independent parallel runs with one index that sets the solver seed, the model restriction (route fixing) and a presolve option (p. 8).
After the first working version, disable or simplify features one at a time until only those that matter remain (p. 5).
Build the ablation arm with the same solver parameters, hardware and parallel layout, only your features off (pp. 9, 11).
Under very short time limits, compare single-thread and multi-thread runs (memory access, turbo boost) (p. 9).
To show what a faster processor would deliver, report the values reached at proportionally longer limits on your hardware, labelled as such (pp. 8-9).

quotes.text: We then followed an inverse path and disabled/simplified the new features until we found which are the ideas that really made a difference.
We soon discovered that the single upper bound on variable zω has a prominent role, in that imposing a tight upper bound on zω triggers the tightening of the domain of many other variables

title: Orbital shrinking: Theory and applications
contribution: Orbital shrinking: aggregating variables along the orbits of (a subgroup of) the formulation's symmetry group gives a relaxation of a convex-objective MINLP, exact for convex problems or when orbit sums are divisible, which a master-slave decomposition with a CP or MIP disaggregation check turns into an exact method; it solves all 120 hard multiple knapsack instances in seconds (CPLEX on the natural model: 65) and beats the explicit regular-language MIP on multi-activity shift scheduling, but loses to the grammar model beyond two activities (read on the author manuscript).
problem_entry: Inverts the MIP and CP reflex of destroying symmetry: keep it as a positive feature, break it only as a last resort; the work traces to an outside question ('Why do you discrete optimization guys hate symmetry and want to destroy it?'); posed as finding a relaxation, the formulation modulo a group, and then an exact method (pp. 1-2, 4, 27).
key_idea: Replace each orbit by one variable equal to its sum, substitute x_j -> z_omega/|omega| in the convex and orbit-sum constraints and the objective, drop the rest: a relaxation (one variable per orbit, one constraint per constraint orbit); the subgroup is a dial between bound and speed; exactness from a logic-Benders-like decomposition whose master aggregates and whose slave checks disaggregation, by CP or MIP (pp. 4-13).
assumptions: MINLP with a convex objective; formulation group computed from a DAG with nauty or saucy; partition into constraints convex in V1 once V2 is fixed and constraints in orbit sums of the pointwise stabilizer; convexity load-bearing (Example 1); 39 symmetric MILPs from Margot's site (23 informative), multi-activity shift scheduling with identical employees from a real store (1-10 activities, 10 each), 120 generated spanner MKP instances with identical knapsacks and identical items (pp. 3-4, 7-9, 13, 18, 21, 23).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: the sum over G of f(pi(j)) equals |G|/|omega| times the sum of f over the orbit, via a bijection between the stabilizer G[j] and T_jl and the orbit-stabilizer theorem, pp. 4-5
Lemma 2 (the group average of a feasible x* equals its orbit averages) and Lemma 3 (orbit sums invariant under G), p. 5

Theorem 1 (the shrunken model is a relaxation): the averaged point satisfies C1 by convexity in V1 and C2 by invariance, z* is integral as a sum of integers, and the objective does not increase by convexity of f over symmetric solutions of equal cost, pp. 5-6
Corollary 1 (exact for convex problems, credited to Gatermann and Parrilo [7]) and Corollary 2 (exact if the orbit sizes divide the orbit sums of some optimal solution and C3 is empty), p. 6
Example 1: (x1 - x2)(x2 - x1) <= -1 is nonempty but its substitution gives 0 <= -1, so convexity is load-bearing, p. 7

Subgroup chain from generators sorted by decreasing number of fixed points, a bound-versus-time dial; automatic choice by relative orbit incidence (8)-(9) closest to 0.82, the mean of hand-picked choices, pp. 8-11

Master-slave decomposition: shrunken master, disaggregation check R(z*) as slave (CP or MIP), rejection by nogood or by branching on integral z with finite convergence for bounded z, cache of checked solutions, variant for continuous variables, pp. 11-13
Correctness safeguard: CPLEX dual reductions disabled when the decomposition runs in callbacks, pp. 18-19, 25

Custom CP propagators (cardinality-based symmetry breaking, shift length) with 2-3 orders of magnitude fewer nodes and less time on hard instances, p. 17; the LP of the Gilmore-Gomory slave detects infeasibility, a Benders nogood from LP duality noted but not implemented, p. 25
experiments: Section 4 (Core 2 Duo 1.4 GHz, CPLEX 12.2): whole group no better than the LP on 31 of 39 and no better than CPLEX's root bound on the other 8; hand-picked subgroups (Table 1) then an automatic rule reported on the same 23 instances (Table 2), strictly above the LP on 13, equal on 8, over the 1800 s cap on 2 by my count, with CPLEX's time to the same bound as yardstick (one loss, cod83). Shift scheduling (Core i5, CPLEX 12.2, Gecode 3.7.3, 1 h, 1% gap): solved hybrid 60 of 100, explicit cpx-reg 28, grammar 98 (grammar numbers copied from another paper, machine and older CPLEX); hybrid gaps below 3%, a tenth of the variables. MKP (CPLEX 12.4, 120 instances, shifted geometric means, same standard packages for all): natural model 65, aggregated items 82, hybrids 110/115/120 solved, the MIP-slave hybrid under four seconds on average; the relaxation closes 42.8-76.7% of the gap in at most 0.031 s. No seeds or repeated runs; no pure-CP baseline although the abstract claims speed-ups over pure MIP or CP (pp. 1, 7-26).
positioning: Against symmetry breaking (Margot's isomorphism pruning and orbits, orbital branching, symmetry in CP); Corollary 1 credited to Gatermann and Parrilo; the decomposition credited as akin to logic-based Benders (Hooker and Ottosson) and to Linderoth, Margot and Thain; Mittelmann and Salvagnin's swapped-role use noted; the grammar model called the current state of the art and kept as the winning baseline; novelty limited to being driven by the automatically detected symmetry group (pp. 2, 4, 6, 11, 13, 15, 19, 27).
writing: Thesis-first contrarian abstract; coined phrase 'formulation modulo a group'; intuition labelled ('Again, intuition led our choice for this feature', 'In our view'); short lemma-theorem-corollary-counterexample theory; losses explained in the body ('This is somehow expected') but absent from the abstract; the conclusion recasts the method as automatic preprocessing that fixes modelling errors (symmetric-cost ATSP) (pp. 1, 4-8, 10, 19, 26).
limits_future: Weak bound with the whole group; the automatic subgroup rule fitted on its evaluation instances; continuous variables make the plain decomposition impractical; the slave keeps the full symmetry; the CP checker needed custom propagators; loses to grammar beyond two activities; LP-duality nogoods unused; future: sufficient conditions for exactness, other symmetric problems (pp. 8-13, 17, 19, 25, 27).

method_links.note: Aggregation along orbits instead of symmetry breaking (one variable per orbit, one constraint per constraint orbit); aggregating identical items alone lifts the solved MKP count from 65 to 82, the hybrid master needs about a tenth of the explicit model's variables, and the symmetric-cost ATSP example shows the method fixing a modelling error. The limitation in SKILL.md is confirmed and sharper: no better than the LP on 31 of 39 and no better than CPLEX's root bound on the other 8; with the automatic subgroup the bound equals the LP on 8 of the 23 informative instances (my count)

The relaxation is solved by black-box CPLEX in default settings, often faster than the original LP; the slaves are stock CP or MIP models, and swapping the CP slave for a MIP one 'did the trick'; the Benders nogood available from LP duality was left out and branching kept as the simpler strategy

The automatic subgroup rule (relative incidence 0.82) is the mean of hand-picked choices on the same 23 instances on which Table 2 then reports it, a lapse SKILL.md dates to 2011 and still present in this 2017 manuscript; grammar's numbers come from another paper, machine and CPLEX version. Counter-evidence: in the MKP study every method uses the same standard packages for a clearer comparison, and master-only node counts are declared
No experiment reports seeds, permutations or repeated runs; the effects claimed are orders of magnitude, so I judge the omission unlikely to change the conclusions

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: monotone dial, then calibrate an automatic setting on hand-picked choices
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Generators ranked by fixed points give a subgroup chain whose bound and time fall almost monotonically; the subgroup is hand-picked per instance by three prioritised criteria, then a structural feature (relative orbit incidence) is set to the mean of the hand-picks, 0.82 (standard deviation 0.17); fitted and reported on the same 23 instances

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: price a relaxation by the stock solver's time to the same bound
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Table 2's 'cpx t' column gives the time CPLEX in default settings needs on the original model to reach the shrunken bound (79.79 s against 3.03 s on cov1075; 9.54 s against 16.78 s on cod83, a loss)

transferable: Get the formulation group automatically: encode the formulation as a DAG and call a graph-automorphism package (nauty, saucy) (pp. 3, 7).

Prove that a symmetry-based reformulation is a relaxation by averaging an arbitrary feasible point over the group and checking each constraint class, and give a two-line counterexample for the load-bearing assumption (pp. 4-7).
Build a subgroup chain by adding generators in decreasing order of fixed points and use it as the bound-versus-time dial (p. 8).
Score candidate orbit partitions by their incidence with constraint supports; low incidence avoids collapsing a constraint into a mere bound (pp. 10-11).

Master on the aggregated model, slave as a disaggregation feasibility check (CP for pure feasibility, MIP where its LP detects infeasibility); reject by nogood or by branching on integral variables, and cache checked aggregated solutions (pp. 12-13, 25).
When a decomposition lives in solver callbacks, switch off the solver features that break its correctness (dual reductions) (pp. 18-19, 25).
Before the exact hybrid phase, solve the aggregated model, repair every aggregated solution within 20% of its optimum, and stop if the gap is already below 1% (p. 18).
Branch first on the variables the check needs in order to be formulated, then run the check with a strict fail limit at nodes to prune (p. 19).
Price a new relaxation by the time the stock solver needs on the original model to reach the same bound, and report the gap closed with its time per class (pp. 11-12, 26).
Compare all methods inside the same standard packages when the scheme is general, and say that this is why specialised codes are left out (p. 23).
coauthors: L. Liberti, D. Salvagnin, T. Walsh (alphabetical list with Fischetti)

quotes.text: In this paper we argue that symmetry is instead a beneficial feature that we should preserve and exploit as much as possible, breaking it only as a last resort.
this approach yields a relaxation bound which is not better than the LP bound 31 times out of 39, and for the remaining 8 times it is not better than the root-node CPLEX’s bound
